1:
That words are said to be seen is noticed by three voices. Henry asks the question and answers it, that God's words are indeed to be seen, as the apostles speak of a word of life they had looked upon and handled, and adds that what was foretold was as certain to the prophet as if seen with his bodily eyes. Calvin makes the same point from the verb, which properly means to see by revelation, and grants the incongruity of speaking of seeing words, noting that one translator paraphrased that they had come to him in a vision, and that the Hebrew has the latitude of the Greek term for word. Gill and Wesley say only that nothing was spoken of himself, all being revealed.

Whether the prophet was rich or poor is the first real dispute. Henry lays out both cases: some think him a rich dealer in cattle, the word being used of a king who was a sheep-master, others a poor keeper who also gathered wild figs; and he draws his moral either way, that God took him as he took David from the flock, choosing the foolish things of the world to confound the wise, so that men are not to be despised for the meanness of their beginnings. Keil and Delitzsch settle it against the wealthy reading: the word signifies a rearer of sheep and not merely an owner, and the prophet elsewhere affirms he was a simple shepherd. Calvin argues the same from the place. He allows the word can mean men possessing flocks who carry on a large business, as the foreign king did by hired shepherds, but denies it fits here, the town being small and of no opulence; and he turns the fact into a rebuke, that by calling himself a shepherd the prophet pours contempt on the pride of king and people, a keeper of sheep being sent to those who would not hear the prophets. Clarke puts him among the very lowest orders of life, tending others' flocks and collecting wild fruit for his own subsistence or to increase his scanty wages. On where he belonged, Clarke breaks with the others: there is no good proof he was a native of the town in Judah, only that he retired there when driven out, and he was very probably born within the northern territories his mission chiefly addressed.

The roar from Zion is heard by each voice in a different register. Clarke regrets that the translators did not keep the verse in its four-line form and observes that the image came naturally to a herdsman familiar with the roaring of lions. Ellicott takes it as the prolonged thunder-peal of the divine voice reverberating from the metropolis to the slopes of the northern promontory, notes that the pastures point back to the prophet's own home in the wilderness, and concludes that the whole country is summoned to listen. Wesley makes it the roar of a hungry lion after prey and gives the geography a polemical edge, Jerusalem being the seat of instituted worship and of the kingdom as God had settled it, from which the ten tribes had revolted in both respects. Calvin presses that contrast hardest. The same words occur in another prophet, he says, but to another purpose: there they set forth God's power against enemies, here they defend pure worship from contempt, with an implied opposition between the one mountain and the rival sanctuaries, so that those who imagined they honoured the God of their fathers with greater displays than at Jerusalem were worshipping their own devices. Keil and Delitzsch pass to the formula that follows and state the rule governing the whole chapter, that the numbers three and four merely denote the multiplicity of the offences, their exact count having no bearing.
3:
Why the oracles begin with the neighbours rather than with Israel is asked and answered twice. Gill gives four reasons: to show Israel the judgments falling on them were not chance, to stop them promising themselves impunity from these nations' prosperity, to awaken them to their danger, and to take off offence at a prophet who began with their enemies. Calvin puts the same thing as an objection before answering it. It seems inconsistent, he says, that one sent to Israel should turn aside to Syria; but had the threatening fallen on Israel alone they might have concluded their sufferings were accidental, since the same evils were overtaking their neighbours, and the prophet's authority would have lost its force unless they were first made to know that God is judge of all nations. Henry supplies the same frame from another prophet's phrase about evil neighbours, and observes that the sin specified in each case is persecution, the measure-filling sin of any people.

The formula of three transgressions and four produces the widest treatment in the chapter and one genuine disagreement. Wesley states it briefly, a certain number put for an uncertain, and Keil and Delitzsch say the same, the numbers denoting multiplicity and their exact count having no bearing. Ellicott adds that the form recurs eight times in these oracles and is idiomatic for repeated delinquencies, and corrects the following clause to read that God will not turn back the judgment he has purposed. Clarke turns the phrase into a small essay on classical usage: he quotes the shipwrecked hero calling those thrice and four times happy who fell at Troy, the Latin poet's version of the cry, an old gloss that this means a finite number for an infinite, and two further instances, concluding that the form is neither infrequent nor inelegant, being used by the most correct writers of antiquity. Henry alone will not settle for the idiomatic reading. He offers it first, then two alternatives: that three and four make seven, a number of perfection, so the measure of their iniquities is full and they are ripe for ruin; or that the three stand for a variety of sins while the fourth is the one specified in each oracle, as elsewhere a list of three things and a fourth singles out the last.

The oracle against Damascus is filled in historically and then disputed geographically. Clarke identifies the successor named and refers the fire to the war afterwards carried on against the Syrians, in which their capital was taken. Gill reads the fire as falling on the house and posterity, naming a later king as perhaps the one meant. Ellicott notes that a later prophet repeats this language when the punishment had already fallen for a while. Calvin observes that a city so fortified might have seemed unassailable, and takes the bar as a part standing for all the strongholds. On the two place-names they divide. Clarke reports on authority that both are names of the valley of Damascus, and identifies the first with a city at the end of the long valley between the two ranges, known to the Greeks as the city of the sun. Ellicott would emend: the word rendered vanity is probably a Masoretic reading and not what the prophet wrote, and it is better to follow the old Greek and read a name referring to the temple then in ruins; the second name he thinks undeterminable, and the bar itself may be used of persons, princes or leaders, as the parallelism supports. Calvin holds both were probably proper names while insisting the prophet alludes to their meanings, so that the plains near Damascus would be emptied of inhabitants. On the place of exile Clarke and Ellicott agree on the river and differ on the region, Clarke placing it on the Caspian, Ellicott east of the upper Euphrates, Wesley in Media.
6:
The offence charged against Gaza is a slave trade, and the voices differ over its scale and occasion. Gill treats the city as standing for the whole nation. Clarke reads the captivity as the fruit of inroads and incursions made in times of peace, and reports the marginal rendering that makes it an entire captivity, all carried off and none afterwards returning. Wesley agrees on the totality, all the captives they had taken, and identifies the buyers as the people's most inveterate enemies, ever ready to enslave and tyrannise over them if they could get them into their hands. Keil and Delitzsch render the phrase as carrying away captives in full number for delivery to that people, and note that the prophet names the one city where the Philistines generally are meant. Calvin fills in the political background: the enemies held that place though it lay within the tribal allotment, their nearness gave them greater opportunity of doing harm, and when they saw the people oppressed they joined their forces to foreign allies.

Calvin then takes a detour into the name of the city and disposes of an etymology. Some think it was so called because a Persian king warring against Egypt deposited his money and valuable furniture there, the Persian word meaning a treasure; Calvin calls this frivolous, both because the Greeks regularly render the Hebrew consonant with their own, so that the form is merely their usual practice, and because the city had the name before that king's time. He prefers to derive it from its strength. He adds a distinction the others do not make, that there were two cities of the name: when the first was demolished the inhabitants built another nearer the sea, which is why a later writer can describe the place as desert, and it is the older city that the prophet threatens, the very destruction predicted here being what moved the city to the shore.

The fire on the wall is then traced through history at very different lengths. Gill offers five fulfilments and chooses none: the king under whom this prophet worked, who broke down the city wall; a later king who smote the Philistines to its borders; the Babylonian conquest foretold by another prophet; the siege by Alexander after the fall of Tyre, the wall undermined and the entry made through its ruins; and the burning of the suburbs in the Maccabean wars. On the neighbouring cities he continues in the same manner, naming for one of them an Assyrian capture and, failing that, its burning in the same later wars, with the temple of its god burnt over those who fled to it and some eight thousand perishing by fire and sword together. Clarke names the five lordships of the Philistines and their position on the coast near Egypt, observing that the others are threatened equally with the first. Wesley notes only that the second city named was a very strong one and shall perish with its king and inhabitants.

Calvin reads the same list for its rhetorical force rather than its fulfilments. That palaces are mentioned shows the city was splendid and sumptuously built, and the point is that neither strength nor wealth would prevent God from executing what its people deserved; the naming of the other cities means that wherever they fled there would be no safe place, since not the capital only but all of them would be exposed as a prey. He infers from the order that one of the cities named was the royal residence though not the metropolis, its pleasant situation having perhaps drawn the king to live there. And when the oracle closes by invoking the name of God, Calvin explains the addition as necessary confirmation, since the Philistines were then in possession of many strong defences and boldly laughed the threatening to scorn.
9:
The brotherly covenant is the crux of this oracle and gets three different referents. Ellicott and Wesley both take it plainly as the league made between the Phoenician king and the two kings of Israel in succession, Ellicott adding that the ancient covenant was forgotten in mercantile cupidity, so that the city was tempted to sell Hebrew captives on to Greeks and Edomites. Clarke offers that reading first and then a rival: some contend that the brotherly covenant means the kinship between the Jews and the Edomites, the two peoples having descended from two brothers, so that cruelties exercised on the one were in effect exercised on the other. Calvin reports the royal friendship, in which the two kings called each other brothers, and then hesitates over it: he does not know whether that view is too strained, and inclines instead to a third, that the offence was delivering up Jews and Israelites to the Edomites when the sellers knew the two peoples to be brethren. From that he draws his moral, that a man who conspires for the ruin of his own brother is a monstrous thing, and that whoever does not abhor a share in such a crime is implicated in it. Keil and Delitzsch make the same relation the whole point of the next oracle, observing that no particular sins are condemned there, only an implacable and mortal hatred towards a brother nation that broke out into cruelty at every opportunity.

When the fire came upon the city is a question the voices answer with different confidence. Gill names three possibilities and settles on none: an Assyrian expedition recorded by the historian, the thirteen-year siege by the Babylonian, or the seven-month siege by Alexander. Clarke combines two of them, making the destructive siege the Babylonian one that lasted thirteen years and ended in the city's destruction, with the final ruin coming from Alexander, and he closes with the state of the place in his own day, only a spot where a few poor fishermen spread their nets. Calvin says outright that when it happened cannot be known with certainty, and then argues against the obvious answer. Both this city and the one named before were demolished by Alexander, but he doubts that is what is meant, since they had suffered long before that; and he supports the doubt with a constitutional observation, that by Alexander's time the city had no king at all but had become a republic in which the people were free and held the chief authority, so that its state and government were wholly different from what they had been. From that change he concludes that the city was laid waste earlier by the Assyrians and afterwards recovered its strength.
11:
Why the Edomites are treated as worse than the heathen is Calvin's whole emphasis. He observes that the nations already condemned had merely delivered the Jews into other hands, whereas these had a common father, bore the same sign of the covenant in circumcision, and were still not made gentle by nearness of blood; and he takes the singular number, which he calls an anomaly since a whole people is meant, as deliberate, the prophet setting two men before us who were really brothers and even twins, so that the barbarity of venting rage against one's own blood may be felt. He guesses that they took arms when the Assyrian came, or perhaps earlier when their neighbours conspired against Judah. On the phrase that follows he reports two constructions besides his own, one rendering it their own bowels and another transferring the pronoun to the sons of Jacob, which he calls strained and improper. Gill supplies the origin of the name from the red pottage for which the birthright was sold. Keil and Delitzsch note that no particular sins are charged here at all, only an implacable mortal hatred towards a brother nation which broke out into cruelty at every opportunity, and render the disputed verb that he stifles his compassion. Ellicott prefers the same rendering, stifled rather than cast off, and offers a fuller reconstruction of the two clauses, that his indignation rended continually and his wrath lurked ever on the watch, while admitting that another punctuation of the Hebrew yields something close to the received version. Wesley reads the same clauses as watching for every occasion to oppress and tearing as a ravenous lion tears its prey. Clarke, who had earlier canvassed a kinship reading of the covenant in the previous oracle, keeps here to history and thinks what the prophet has in view is most probably the part these people took in distressing the Jews when Jerusalem was besieged and finally taken.

The two cities named at the close are located and characterised at very different depths. Clarke is content with eight words, that they are principal cities of the country. Wesley makes the first the metropolis, named from a grandson of Esau, and the second a very strong city and one of the chief in the kingdom, so that in threatening both the strength and the glory of the nation is threatened with utter overthrow. Gill agrees on the descent of the name, adds that two ancient authorities knew a village of the name five miles from the rock city which held a Roman garrison, notes that the word is put for the whole country, and observes that it signifies the south. Ellicott brings the literary associations: the wisdom and might of that people were well known, and one of the sage interlocutors in the book of Job came from there; he cites two modern travellers for its position south of a certain valley, distinguishes the second city carefully from another of the same name in Moab, and identifies it with a modern village on the authority of the same two travellers.
13:
The atrocity charged against the Ammonites is agreed to be unrecorded elsewhere, and the voices differ only in how they fill the gap. Clarke says it refers to some barbarous transaction well known in the prophet's time but of which the sacred historians give no distinct mention. Ellicott says the same and supplies the context instead, that the barbarous modes of warfare then prevailing are darkly conveyed in several other passages and throughout the Assyrian inscriptions. Keil and Delitzsch offer a guess at the occasion, that it may have happened during the Syrian wars against Israel, when these people took the opportunity to widen their territory by conquest. Gill and Calvin both trace the kinship that aggravates the crime, Gill from the descent through Lot and Calvin more elaborately, that Lot was counted a son of Abraham and brought up as one, so that Abraham was the common father of both nations and their joining forces with enemies admitted of no excuse. Calvin adds that many other crimes could have been charged, only one being singled out in passing while the general declaration is that the people were past hope.

Calvin then reports and refuses an emendation that would remove the atrocity altogether. Some read the word for pregnant women as mountains, driven to it, he thinks, only because they find it strange that women should be ripped up merely to extend a border; on that reading they had cut through mountains and the earth itself, no obstacle standing in the way of an insatiable cupidity that destroyed the whole order of nature. Others, he says, take the mountains metaphorically for fortified cities, since cities stand in a conqueror's way as mountains do; and that exposition he calls too strained. His own judgment is that the word bears its genuine and usual sense, as it plainly does in another prophet. Wesley states the motive without the horror, that the border was enlarged by destroying all who dwelt in it and might hereafter claim a title to it.

The last verse turns on a single word, and the three positions are clean. Clarke thinks the word rendered their king should probably be read as the name of the national god, and that the princes who go with him may then be the body of his priesthood. Ellicott names the versions that read it so and rejects them: the received rendering is supported by the old Greek, by the Targum, and by the context of the passage. Gill gives both readings without choosing, identifying on the first the last king of that people, accessory to the murder of the governor set over the remnant of the Jews and so perhaps provoking the expedition that destroyed his capital; and observing on the second that conquerors commonly carried away the gods of the nations they subdued, with two classical examples of gods taken as spoil and carried in triumphs. Calvin decides it by the wording: some regard it as a proper name because the idol bore it, but since the text says their king, he and his princes, the prophet doubtless means the king, whom he joins with his nobles. He is candid that the prediction's fulfilment, though he does not doubt it, has left no history extant. On the fire itself Gill names the Babylonian as the likely enemy and Clarke says the subjection was total and was his work, while Ellicott notes that a later prophet gives a vivid account of the same doom, quoting and expanding this very passage. Ellicott also draws the conclusion of the whole series, that the prophet has been denouncing the sin which trifles with blood, covenants and ancient agreements, and recognising the responsibilities of race, but that closer inspection shows him condemning every violation of those natural laws and rights of which he regards God as the custodian and executor.
